--- title: "Hyperparameter selection" description: "A setting such as a tree's node size must be chosen on data the model was not fitted to. Cross-validation by site lets every training site take a turn as new data, and gives a steadier verdict than one set of validation sites." order: 6 categories: [generalisation, tuning] --- ## Settings the fitting cannot choose Each page in this section has turned a setting, a tree's minimum node size or the lasso's penalty λ, and found that its best value cannot be read from the training error. This page names those settings and introduces **cross-validation**, the standard way to choose them. It also shows that one set of validation sites, as earlier sections used, gives a verdict that swings with the sites that happen to be held back. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Parameters and hyperparameters A **parameter** is learned by fitting: the coefficients of a regression, or the splits of a tree and the prediction in each leaf. A **hyperparameter** is fixed before fitting begins, and limits what the fitting can do: a tree's depth or minimum node size, the number of trees in a forest, the penalty λ. The fitting cannot choose a hyperparameter, because on its own data the most flexible setting always looks best, as [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) showed. It has to be chosen on data the model was not fitted to. [Splitting the data](../02-marine-data/splitting-data.qmd) gave that job to validation data: fit the model at each candidate setting, score it on the validation sites, and keep the setting that scores best. The test sites are kept for one final score of the chosen model. But one set of validation sites is a small sample, and a different set could favour a different setting. ## Cross-validation gives every site a turn as new data **k-fold cross-validation** lets the training data take turns as the validation data. It cuts the training sites into *k* groups, called **folds**. In each of *k* rounds, one fold is held out, the model is fitted to the other *k* − 1, and the held-out fold is scored as new sites. Every training site is scored once, by a model that was not fitted to it, and the *k* errors are averaged. That average, the **cross-validated error**, is worked out for every candidate setting, and the setting with the lowest one is chosen. ::: {.diagram} ![The training sites are cut into five folds. In each of five rounds a different fold is held out and scored as new sites, while the model is fitted to the other four. The five errors are averaged. This is repeated for every candidate setting; the best is refitted on all the training sites, and the test sites are scored once at the end.](img/hyperparameter-selection.svg){fig-alt="A card shows the training sites cut into five folds, each fold a block of four sites. In five rounds, a different fold is held out and scored as new sites while the model is fitted to the other four, giving errors one to five. The five errors are averaged to give the setting's cross-validated error. Below, four steps: repeat for every candidate setting; choose the setting with the lowest average; refit it on all the training sites; score the test sites once, at the end. A note says each fold holds whole sites, so no site is fitted to and scored in the same round."} ::: The folds hold whole sites, for the reason the split does: visits to one site resemble each other, so a site on both sides would score the model on a place it has already seen. Five or ten folds are usual. With more folds, each round fits to more of the data, but there is more fitting to do: every candidate setting is fitted once per fold. Anything learned from the data belongs inside the rounds, including the preprocessing. The median that fills a gap is worked out again from each round's fitting folds, which a workflow does by itself; worked out once from all the training sites, it would leak the held-out fold into the fitting ([Avoiding information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd)). ## Worked example The data, split by site, and the tree are those of [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd), and so are the 12 minimum node sizes. That page averaged 20 random splits of the training sites; here the training sites are cut into ten folds instead. The test sites are scored at the very end. ### Preparing the folds ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) # ten folds of training sites folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10) predictors <- abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu + substrate + season tree_recipe <- recipe(predictors, data = train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) leaves_of <- function(fitted) sum(extract_fit_engine(fitted)$frame$var == "") held_out <- map(folds$splits, assessment) tibble(folds = length(held_out), `sites in a fold` = n_distinct(held_out[[1]]$site_id), `fewest stations` = min(map_int(held_out, nrow)), `most stations` = max(map_int(held_out, nrow))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| folds| sites in a fold| fewest stations| most stations| |-----:|---------------:|---------------:|-------------:| | 10| 12| 49| 74|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() numeric = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] categorical = ["substrate", "season"] predictors = numeric + categorical grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train, test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] # ten folds of training sites folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=123) tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([ ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric), ("categorical", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False), categorical), ]) # rpart also keeps every leaf at a third of min_n or more; this matches it. def tree_pipeline(min_n): model = DecisionTreeRegressor(min_samples_split=min_n, min_samples_leaf=max(1, round(min_n / 3)), random_state=123) return Pipeline([("recipe", tree_recipe), ("model", model)]) held_out = [train.iloc[new_rows] for fit_rows, new_rows in folds.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])] pd.DataFrame({"folds": [len(held_out)], "sites in a fold": [held_out[0]["site_id"].nunique()], "fewest stations": [min(len(h) for h in held_out)], "most stations": [max(len(h) for h in held_out)]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | folds | sites in a fold | fewest stations | most stations | |--------:|------------------:|------------------:|----------------:| | 10 | 12 | 47 | 69 | ::: ::: ::: The 120 training sites make ten folds of 12. The folds hold different numbers of stations, because some sites were visited more often than others. ### Every node size scored in every fold `tune()` marks the setting to be filled in later, and `tune_grid()` fits and scores the workflow at every candidate value in every fold: 12 values in ten folds, 120 trees. Each fold also gets the error of predicting its fitting folds' average count, as a baseline. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sizes <- c(300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2) # The depth limit is set high so that min_n alone sets the size of the tree. tree_model <- decision_tree(mode = "regression", tree_depth = 30, min_n = tune(), cost_complexity = 0) tree_workflow <- workflow(tree_recipe, tree_model) tuned <- tune_grid(tree_workflow, resamples = folds, grid = tibble(min_n = sizes), metrics = metric_set(rmse), control = control_grid(extract = leaves_of)) # the baseline: predict each round's fitting average for its held-out sites average <- map_dbl(folds$splits, \(s) { rmse_vec(assessment(s)$abundance, rep(mean(analysis(s)$abundance), nrow(assessment(s)))) }) collect_metrics(tuned) |> select(min_n, mean, std_err) |> arrange(desc(min_n)) |> mutate(across(c(mean, std_err), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| min_n| mean| std_err| |-----:|----:|-------:| | 300| 4.69| 0.35| | 200| 4.65| 0.36| | 130| 4.74| 0.35| | 80| 4.73| 0.28| | 50| 4.78| 0.31| | 30| 4.72| 0.22| | 20| 4.94| 0.21| | 13| 5.22| 0.21| | 8| 5.59| 0.35| | 5| 5.93| 0.29| | 3| 6.28| 0.39| | 2| 6.44| 0.37|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} sizes = [300, 200, 130, 80, 50, 30, 20, 13, 8, 5, 3, 2] # The two tree settings move together, so each candidate is its own small grid. grid = [{"model__min_samples_split": [n], "model__min_samples_leaf": [max(1, round(n / 3))]} for n in sizes] tuned = GridSearchCV(tree_pipeline(2), grid, cv=folds, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error") tuned = tuned.fit(train[predictors], train["abundance"], groups=train["site_id"]) # One row per setting, one column per fold. The standard error is the folds' # standard deviation over the root of the number of folds, as tidymodels has it. fold_errors = -np.column_stack([tuned.cv_results_[f"split{k}_test_score"] for k in range(10)]) metrics = pd.DataFrame({ "min_n": sizes, "mean": fold_errors.mean(axis=1), "std_err": fold_errors.std(axis=1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(10), }) metrics.round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | min_n | mean | std_err | |--------:|-------:|----------:| | 300 | 4.19 | 0.34 | | 200 | 4.14 | 0.33 | | 130 | 4.2 | 0.33 | | 80 | 4.21 | 0.29 | | 50 | 4.36 | 0.31 | | 30 | 4.32 | 0.3 | | 20 | 4.66 | 0.31 | | 13 | 4.82 | 0.31 | | 8 | 5.05 | 0.3 | | 5 | 5.45 | 0.34 | | 3 | 5.7 | 0.31 | | 2 | 5.67 | 0.31 | ::: ::: ::: In the table, `mean` is the cross-validated error: the average of the ten folds' RMSEs. `std_err` is its **standard error**, a measure of how far that average could move with a different draw of sites. It is the spread of the ten fold errors divided by the square root of ten. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(cv, aes(leaves, mean)) + geom_hline(yintercept = baseline, linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_hline(yintercept = cut_off, linetype = "dotted") + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - std_err, ymax = mean + std_err), width = 0.05, colour = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + geom_line(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], linewidth = 1) + geom_point(colour = ml_palette[["blue"]], size = 2) + geom_point(data = best_row, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 4) + annotate("text", x = max(cv$leaves), y = baseline, label = "predict the average", hjust = 1, vjust = 1.6, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], size = 3.4) + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "Leaves in the tree (log scale)", y = "Cross-validated RMSE (individuals)", title = "The bottom of the curve is flat: many node sizes tie") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cross-validated error of trees with 12 minimum node sizes, against the average number of leaves they grew. The bars reach one standard error either side. The dotted line is one standard error above the lowest point; the dashed line is the error of predicting the average.](hyperparameter-selection_files/figure-html/fig-cv-1.png){#fig-cv fig-alt='Points joined by a line show cross-validated RMSE against the number of leaves on a log scale, each with a vertical error bar. From the left, at about 3 leaves, the error stays within one standard error of the lowest up to about 47 leaves, then climbs steadily to 6.44 at about 376 leaves. The lowest point, 4.65, is marked at about 5 leaves. A dotted line one standard error above it, at 5.01, sits above seven of the points. A dashed line for predicting the average is at 4.91.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### Many node sizes tie and the simplest is chosen The lowest cross-validated error is 4.65, for a node size of 200 and trees of about 5 leaves, the same setting [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd) found. Predicting the average scores 4.91. But the bottom of the curve is flat: seven of the 12 settings, from about 3 to 47 leaves, lie within one standard error of the lowest. The data cannot tell those settings apart. A common way to break the tie is the **one-standard-error rule**: among the settings within one standard error of the lowest, take the simplest. Here, that is a node size of 300. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} best <- select_best(tuned, metric = "rmse") simplest <- select_by_one_std_err(tuned, desc(min_n), metric = "rmse") bind_rows(`lowest error` = best, `one-standard-error rule` = simplest, .id = "rule") |> select(rule, min_n) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|rule | min_n| |:-----------------------|-----:| |lowest error | 200| |one-standard-error rule | 300|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} lowest = metrics.loc[metrics["mean"].idxmin()] within = metrics["mean"] <= lowest["mean"] + lowest["std_err"] # Larger nodes make smaller trees, so the simplest tied setting has the largest min_n. pd.DataFrame({"rule": ["lowest error", "one-standard-error rule"], "min_n": [int(lowest["min_n"]), int(metrics.loc[within, "min_n"].max())]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | rule | min_n | |:------------------------|--------:| | lowest error | 200 | | one-standard-error rule | 300 | ::: ::: ::: `desc(min_n)` tells `select_by_one_std_err()` which way is simpler: a larger node size makes a smaller tree. The rule trades a little of the error for a simpler model, on the grounds that the more flexible model's lead is within the noise. ### One validation split gives a noisy verdict The choice above rests on one cutting of the sites into folds. To see how much a choice depends on the sites that happen to be held out, the whole selection is repeated 40 times, in two ways. One uses a single validation split, three quarters of the training sites for fitting, as in [Decision trees](../03-supervised-learning/decision-trees.qmd). The other uses ten-fold cross-validation, with the sites dealt into new folds each time. Each run records the node size that won and the error it claimed. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # The error on the held-out sites of each node size, fitted to the rest errors_on <- function(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) new <- assessment(s) map_dbl(sizes, \(n) { fitted <- finalize_workflow(tree_workflow, tibble(min_n = n)) |> fit(fitting) rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new)$.pred) }) } winner <- function(errors) tibble(min_n = sizes[which.min(errors)], claimed = min(errors)) repeats <- map(1:40, \(r) { one_split <- group_initial_split(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) ten_folds <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10) # one column per fold; the row means are the cross-validated errors fold_errors <- sapply(ten_folds$splits, errors_on) bind_rows(`One validation split` = winner(errors_on(one_split)), `Ten-fold cross-validation` = winner(rowMeans(fold_errors)), .id = "method") }) |> list_rbind() repeats |> summarise(`different winners` = n_distinct(min_n), `lowest claimed` = min(claimed), `highest claimed` = max(claimed), .by = method) |> mutate(across(contains("claimed"), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|method | different winners| lowest claimed| highest claimed| |:-------------------------|-----------------:|--------------:|---------------:| |One validation split | 7| 3.52| 6.36| |Ten-fold cross-validation | 5| 4.45| 4.70|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} def errors_on(fit_rows, new_rows): fitting, new = train.iloc[fit_rows], train.iloc[new_rows] fitted = [tree_pipeline(n).fit(fitting[predictors], fitting["abundance"]) for n in sizes] return np.array([root_mean_squared_error(new["abundance"], f.predict(new[predictors])) for f in fitted]) runs = [] for r in range(40): one_split = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=r) ten_folds = GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=r) groups = train["site_id"] one = errors_on(*next(one_split.split(train, groups=groups))) ten = np.mean([errors_on(*f) for f in ten_folds.split(train, groups=groups)], axis=0) for method, errors in [("One validation split", one), ("Ten-fold cross-validation", ten)]: runs.append({"method": method, "min_n": sizes[errors.argmin()], "claimed": errors.min()}) repeats = pd.DataFrame(runs) (repeats.groupby("method", sort=False) .agg(**{"different winners": ("min_n", "nunique"), "lowest claimed": ("claimed", "min"), "highest claimed": ("claimed", "max")}) .reset_index() .round(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | method | different winners | lowest claimed | highest claimed | |:--------------------------|--------------------:|-----------------:|------------------:| | One validation split | 7 | 3.23 | 5.17 | | Ten-fold cross-validation | 3 | 3.97 | 4.21 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} repeats |> mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("One validation split", "Ten-fold cross-validation")), min_n = factor(min_n, levels = sizes)) |> ggplot(aes(min_n, claimed, colour = method)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0, seed = 1), size = 2, alpha = 0.7, show.legend = FALSE) + facet_wrap(~ method, ncol = 1) + scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(ml_palette[["vermilion"]], ml_palette[["blue"]])) + labs(x = "Minimum node size chosen (rigid on the left, flexible on the right)", y = "RMSE claimed for the winner (individuals)", title = "One validation split gives a noisy verdict") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The node size chosen in each of 40 runs, and the error claimed for it, by a single validation split (top) and by ten-fold cross-validation (bottom). Node sizes run from rigid on the left to flexible on the right.](hyperparameter-selection_files/figure-html/fig-repeats-1.png){#fig-repeats fig-alt='Two panels of points share an axis of the 12 node sizes, from 300 on the left to 2 on the right. Each point is one run, placed at the node size it chose and the error it claimed. With one validation split, the points spread over 7 node sizes, from 300 to 20, and from 3.52 to 6.36 in error. With ten-fold cross-validation, they sit over 5 node sizes, from 300 to 50, in a narrow band from 4.45 to 4.70. No run chose a node size smaller than 20.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: **One validation split gives a noisy verdict.** Across the 40 runs, the error it claimed for its winner ranged from 3.52 to 6.36, a spread caused only by which sites were held out. That spread is about 11 times the tree's whole lead over predicting the average. Ten-fold cross-validation's claimed errors ranged only from 4.45 to 4.70: each rests on every training site, not a quarter of them. **Both choices wander within the flat bottom.** One validation split chose seven different node sizes, from 300 down to 20. Cross-validation chose five, and settled on 200 in 18 of the 40 runs. Every one of the 80 choices was among the settings that tie, so neither method can pin the node size down, and the data say it matters little. The claimed error is also a little flattering. It is the lowest of 12 errors, so part of the winner's lead is luck. The honest figure comes from data that played no part in the choice: the test sites. ### Scoring the test sites once `last_fit()` refits the chosen workflow on all the training sites and scores the test sites. It is the only step on this page that touches them, and it comes after the choice is made. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} final <- tree_workflow |> finalize_workflow(best) |> last_fit(split, metrics = metric_set(rmse)) test <- testing(split) tibble(model = c("decision tree", "predict the average"), `test sites` = c(collect_metrics(final)$.estimate, rmse_vec(test$abundance, rep(mean(train$abundance), nrow(test))))) |> mutate(`test sites` = round(`test sites`, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | test sites| |:-------------------|----------:| |decision tree | 3.80| |predict the average | 4.08|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # GridSearchCV has already refitted its best setting on all the training sites. final = tuned.best_estimator_ pd.DataFrame({ "model": ["decision tree", "predict the average"], "test sites": [ root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], final.predict(test[predictors])), root_mean_squared_error(test["abundance"], np.full(len(test), train["abundance"].mean())), ], }).round(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | test sites | |:--------------------|-------------:| | decision tree | 5.19 | | predict the average | 5.55 | ::: ::: ::: The tree scores 3.80 on the test sites, against 4.08 for predicting the training sites' average: better by 0.29. Cross-validation put the tree 0.26 ahead of the average. Both errors are lower on the test sites than in cross-validation, because these 40 sites happen to be easier to predict; a single set of test sites is one draw too. The gain over the average on the same sites is the fairer comparison, and it holds up. Once the test sites have been scored, they are spent. Choosing again because their score disappointed would make them validation sites, and the score would flatter the model as the claimed errors above do. [Cross-validation](../07-validation/cross-validation.qmd), in section 7, shows how to get an honest score when the data are too few to set test sites aside. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A **hyperparameter** is fixed before fitting and limits it. The training error always favours the most flexible setting, so a hyperparameter is chosen on data the model was not fitted to. - **k-fold cross-validation** cuts the training data into *k* folds; each takes a turn as new data while the model is fitted to the rest, and the *k* errors are averaged. Folds hold whole sites, as a split does. - **One validation split gives a noisy verdict.** In 40 runs, the error it claimed for its winner ranged from 3.52 to 6.36; with ten-fold cross-validation, from 4.45 to 4.70. - Settings within one standard error of the best cannot be told apart. The **one-standard-error rule** takes the simplest of them. - In tidymodels: `tune()`, `group_vfold_cv()`, `tune_grid()`, `select_best()`, `finalize_workflow()`, then `last_fit()`, the only step that scores the test sites. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Replace `group_vfold_cv()` with `vfold_cv(train, v = 10)`, which deals stations into folds regardless of their site. Does the cross-validated error fall, and does the chosen tree get more flexible? 2. Tune the lasso of [Regularisation](regularisation.qmd) on these folds, with `linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 1) |> set_engine("glmnet")` and a grid of λ from 0.001 to 10. The recipe needs `step_dummy()` for substrate and season, and `step_normalize()`. Which inputs does the lasso keep at the chosen λ?
